d.title: Six classes at a million items, from 0.0001 ms to three hours
d.caption: **Complexity notation says nothing about whether a function takes a microsecond or a minute — it describes how the cost changes as the input grows, and deliberately discards the constant factors, the hardware and the language.** Which makes it narrow and makes the last column worth memorising: **at n = 1,000,000 and 100 ns a step, `O(n)` is 100 ms and `O(n²)` is three hours.** That gap is the entire practical content of the topic — **the difference between a request and an outage, from one scan moved inside a loop.**

d.title: The time ratio when you double n *is* the exponent, and it takes thirty seconds
d.caption: **You do not have to derive complexity from source — run the code at n, then at 2n, and the ratio of the times is the growth class.** The measured run is unambiguous: **×3.95, ×4.00, ×4.03 across three doublings, which is `O(n²)` and not an argument anybody needs to win.** And the table's value is the last column: **a ratio near 2.0 means reduce the constant factor, near 2.2 is usually a sort and normal, and near 4.0 means find the scan inside the loop — which is the fix worth making.**

state: stop - size is not the problem
find the scan inside the loop

d.title: The growth is not 1.125x per resize — it is 32, then 64, then 96 bytes at a time
d.caption: **A list owns a block of slots; when it fills, CPython allocates a larger block and copies every element across — so that individual append is `O(n)`, and only the average over the whole sequence is constant.** Which is what *amortised* promises and what it does not: **it says nothing about any single call.** The measured steps show the over-allocation growing with the list — **+32 bytes early and +800 at length 761** — so **a latency-sensitive loop can hit a copy of the whole list at an unpredictable moment, and `O(1) amortised` will not warn you.**

d.title: Four situations where growth is the wrong lens, and the last one is not an operation at all
d.caption: **This is the part that separates people who quote big-O from people who use it.** The second row is the one that overturns intuition: **an `O(n)` loop making one HTTP call per item is 100× slower than an `O(n²)` loop doing arithmetic, at every realistic n.** And the fourth is a category error rather than a trade: **complexity counts operations, and waiting on a socket is not an operation — it is 200 ms of nothing**, so the lens to use is round-trip count and concurrency.

two array passes beat one pointer chase

d.title: Everyone picked json.loads; 58% was in strptime
d.caption: **`json.loads` is about 16% of the runtime and roughly 58% is in `datetime.strptime` — a function nobody had an opinion about.** The reason is mechanical and worth knowing: **`strptime` builds and matches a regular expression derived from your format string on every single call**, so 200,000 lines means 200,000 regex compilations' worth of work. Which is why the lesson is framed as predict-then-measure: **the prediction was not close, and no amount of reading the source would have produced the real answer.**

d.title: cProfile stops at function boundaries
d.caption: **When the expensive function is one of yours and forty lines long, a function-level profile tells you the name you already suspected and nothing more** — which is where the next resolution down earns its place. `line_profiler` attributes time **per line, inside the function you nominate**, at the cost of running under its decorator. And for the case where the process is already running and you cannot restart it: **`py-spy` samples a live process without stopping it or importing into it**, which is the only option in production.

nodes.label: At the cost of its decorator
Which is the only production option

d.title: Making a 30% part infinitely fast buys 1.4x
d.caption: **A part's share of the runtime caps what any optimisation of it can ever return, and the arithmetic is worth doing before you commit a week.** The rows that matter are the bottom three: **at 30% of runtime, making the part *infinitely* fast buys 1.4× — and at 10% it buys 1.1×.** Which is the number to compute before starting, because **a 2× speedup of a 5% part is a 1.03× speedup of the program**, and that is three days of work for something nobody can measure in production.

d.title: Six tools, and the obvious one is useful for almost nothing
d.caption: **`sys.getsizeof` measures one object shallowly — so a list of a million strings reports 8,856 bytes, the size of the pointer array, and not the strings.** Which is why the measured numbers sit beside each other: **48, 104, 8,856 shallow against 184,320 deep.** The default is `tracemalloc`, because **it attributes allocations to the line that made them**, and the escalation is `memray` **for when `tracemalloc` shows nothing — which means the allocation happened in a C extension it cannot see.**

state: sizing a structure you are choosing
the whole process, as the OS sees it

d.title: One row of this table is the whole accidental quadratic
d.caption: **`x in c` is `O(n)` on a list and `O(1)` on a set — and that single difference, inside a loop, is the commonest quadratic in production Python.** The rest of the table is the cost of switching: **a set has no order and no duplicates, so it is not a drop-in replacement for a list you are also iterating.** Which is why the usual fix is **both** — 2.8's “hold the data twice” — and why `deque` is the answer to a different quadratic: **removing from the front of a list is `O(n)` and `O(1)` on a deque.**

steps.code: insert or remove at the front

d.title: NumPy indexed element by element was slower than plain Python
d.caption: **4.10 s for the Python loop, 9.80 s for the same loop indexing a NumPy array, and 0.031 s vectorised — so the middle row is 2.4× *slower* than doing nothing at all.** The reason is the whole lesson: **indexing a NumPy array from Python pays a boxing cost per element on top of the interpreter overhead the loop already had**, so you have added work without removing any. **NumPy is not a faster list — it is a way of moving the loop out of Python**, and if the loop stays, it is a pessimisation.

d.title: Four routes into native code, and the row that is not about speed
d.caption: **Memory safety is the row that actually differentiates them: Cython and a hand-written C extension are yours to get right, and Rust's is enforced** — which is a correctness argument rather than a performance one, since all three reach similar speeds. The honest ordering by cost: **Cython is annotated Python with a low learning cost, `ctypes`/`cffi` needs no build chain at all because the library already exists, and both C and Rust are a high learning cost plus `cibuildwheel` or `maturin` for every platform.**

columns.title: Low cost to adopt
items: Cython — annotated Python, a compiler, low learning cost
ctypes / cffi — no build chain; the .so already exists
both leave memory safety to you
Cython needs cibuildwheel for wheels; cffi needs nothing

columns.title: High cost, more to show for it
items: C extension — the CPython API directly, high learning cost
Rust + PyO3 — high learning cost, memory safety ENFORCED
maturin makes Rust wheels well supported
and all four reach broadly similar speeds
